short_title: NCIP v. Macroasia Corporation (Judgment on Compromise)
full_title: NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INDIGENOUS PEOPLES (NCIP), ZENAIDA BRIGIDA HAMADA-PAWID, DIONESIA O. BANUA, CONCHITA C. CALZADO, PERCY BRAWNER, COSME LAMBAYON, SANTOS UNSAD, AND BASILIO WANDAG, PETITIONERS, VS. MACROASIA CORPORATION, RESPONDENT.
subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
syllabus_topic: VIII. Obligations and Contracts > B. Contracts > 1. General Provisions > b. Fundamental Principles > i. Autonomy
topics: Judgment based on a compromise agreement while a petition is pending before the Supreme Court
Test for approval: not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy and public order
Compromise by a government agency, with the OSG joining the motion
FPIC and Certification Precondition under RA 8371 (background only)

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > R. Judgments and Final Orders > 3. How Rendered (Rule 36)

doctrine:
No new doctrine. **Parties to a case pending before the Supreme Court may settle it through a compromise agreement and jointly move for judgment based on it. The Court will approve and adopt the compromise if it was validly executed and is not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy and public order.** It will then enjoin the parties to comply with its terms in utmost good faith and declare the case closed and terminated. The Court applied this test without reviewing the merits of the CA ruling under appeal.

A government agency may enter into such a compromise. Here the NCIP signed through its Chairperson, and the Office of the Solicitor General joined the motion for judgment. The decision cites no Civil Code provision. The test it applied matches the general limits on contractual stipulations (Civil Code, Art. 1306) and the nature of a compromise as a contract that ends a pending litigation (Civil Code, Art. 2028).
facts:
Macroasia Corporation held Mineral Production Sharing Agreement (MPSA) No. 220-2005-IVB, issued in December 2005, covering 1,114 hectares in Barangays Ipilan, Mambalot and Maasin, Brooke's Point, Palawan. Its application for mining permits was endorsed to the NCIP for the Free and Prior Informed Consent (FPIC) process, which is required for the issuance of a Certification Precondition. After the FPIC process with the Pala'wan communities, a Joint Resolution of Consent and a Memorandum of Agreement were executed on April 21, 2010, and the FPIC and validation teams recommended issuance of the Certification Precondition. The NCIP En Banc, however, denied it in Resolution No. 001-2012, mainly because a separate field-based investigation (FBI) was required for two indirectly affected barangays, Aribungos and Barong-barong. It denied reconsideration on February 23, 2012.

On Macroasia's petition for review, the CA issued an Amended Decision dated March 14, 2016 directing the NCIP to issue the Certification Precondition, and denied reconsideration on August 9, 2016. The NCIP and its officials filed a Rule 45 petition with the Supreme Court.

While the petition was pending, Macroasia assigned its MPSA rights to Macroasia Mining Corporation on June 7, 2019, and the DENR Secretary approved the assignment on February 1, 2021. In August 2022 Macroasia Mining conducted a separate FBI/FPIC process for Aribungos and Barong-barong, which ended in a Memorandum of Agreement with the IP leaders. On February 1, 2023 the NCIP and Macroasia Mining, acting as assignee and authorized representative of Macroasia, signed a Compromise Agreement. In it the parties acknowledged that the FPIC process had been properly conducted and validated and that all five barangays had issued Joint Resolutions of Consent. Macroasia Mining undertook to keep securing all required permits, and the NCIP undertook to keep reviewing its processes. The parties agreed to move for dismissal of the case with prejudice. Macroasia filed a Joint Motion to Render Judgment Based on Compromise Agreement dated February 21, 2023, which the OSG joined on behalf of the NCIP on March 30, 2023.
issues: Whether the Compromise Agreement may be approved and judgment rendered on it, terminating the petition.
ruling:
**1. Yes.** The Court reproduced the Compromise Agreement in full and found it "validly executed and not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy, and public order." It granted the Joint Motion to Render Judgment Based on Compromise Agreement, approved and adopted the agreement, enjoined the parties to comply with its terms in utmost good faith, and declared the case closed and terminated.

The Court did not rule on whether the CA's Amended Decision was correct or on any issue under RA 8371. The dispute ended on the parties' own settlement. Under that settlement, the FPIC for the two indirectly affected barangays, which was the main reason the NCIP had denied the Certification Precondition, had already been conducted.
disposition: The Joint Motion to Render Judgment Based on Compromise Agreement was GRANTED. The Compromise Agreement dated February 1, 2023 was APPROVED and ADOPTED, the parties were ENJOINED to comply with its terms in utmost good faith, and the case was deemed CLOSED and TERMINATED.

bar_questions.q: A government agency filed a Rule 45 petition against a mining company in the Supreme Court. While it was pending, the agency, represented by its chairperson, and the company signed a compromise agreement settling the dispute and filed a joint motion for judgment based on it; the Office of the Solicitor General joined the motion. (a) May the Supreme Court render judgment on the compromise instead of deciding the petition on the merits? (b) What must the Court determine before approving it?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. (b) The Court must find that the compromise was validly executed and is not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy and public order.
alac.legal_basis: A compromise is a contract by which the parties, through reciprocal concessions, avoid a litigation or end one already begun (Civil Code, Art. 2028). Contracting parties may agree on terms they consider convenient, provided these are not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public order or public policy (Civil Code, Art. 1306). In NCIP v. Macroasia Corporation (G.R. No. 226176, August 9, 2023), the Supreme Court acted on a joint motion filed while a Rule 45 petition was pending and joined by the OSG for the government agency. It found the compromise "validly executed and not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy, and public order," approved and adopted it, enjoined compliance in utmost good faith, and declared the case closed and terminated.
alac.application: The case is still pending, so the parties may end it by compromise. The agency acted through its chairperson, and the OSG joined the motion. If the Court finds the agreement validly executed and its terms consistent with law, morals, good customs, public policy and public order, it will approve the agreement, render judgment on it, and close the case without ruling on the merits of the appeal.
alac.conclusion: The Supreme Court may render judgment on the compromise once it is shown to be valid and not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy or public order.

bar_questions.q: Same facts as in the previous problem, but the compromise provides that the agency will issue the mining company a Certification Precondition over land within an ancestral domain even though the indigenous cultural communities concerned have not given their free and prior informed consent (FPIC). Should the Supreme Court approve the compromise?

alac.answer: No. A compromise that dispenses with a requirement of law is contrary to law and public policy and cannot be approved.
alac.legal_basis: The Court approves a compromise only if it is "validly executed and not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy, and public order" (NCIP v. Macroasia Corporation, G.R. No. 226176, August 9, 2023; see Civil Code, Art. 1306). Under Section 59 of RA 8371 (IPRA), the NCIP may not issue a Certification Precondition without the free and prior informed and written consent of the ICCs/IPs concerned. The compromise in Macroasia itself described the FPIC process as a requirement for the issuance of the Certification Precondition.
alac.application: In Macroasia, the parties acknowledged before settling that the FPIC process had been conducted and validated for all the affected barangays. This compromise, by contrast, would have the agency issue the certification without FPIC. That term violates IPRA and the public policy of protecting the rights of indigenous peoples, so the agreement fails the test for approval.
alac.conclusion: The Supreme Court should refuse to approve the compromise and should resolve the petition on its merits.

bar_questions.q: The Supreme Court approved a compromise agreement between Agency X and Company Y and declared the case closed and terminated. Under the compromise, the parties had agreed to the dismissal with prejudice of X's pending petition. A year later, X's new chairperson filed a new case against Y raising the same claims that the compromise had settled. Will the new case prosper?

alac.answer: No. The judicial compromise has the effect of res judicata between the parties, and the case it settled was closed and terminated with prejudice.
alac.legal_basis: A compromise has upon the parties the effect and authority of res judicata (Civil Code, Art. 2037). In NCIP v. Macroasia Corporation (G.R. No. 226176, August 9, 2023), the Court approved and adopted a compromise in which the parties agreed to the dismissal with prejudice of the pending petition. It enjoined them to comply with the agreement in utmost good faith and declared the case closed and terminated.
alac.application: Agency X, through its chairperson at the time, freely entered into the compromise, and the Supreme Court approved it and rendered judgment on it. The agency is the party bound, regardless of any change in its leadership. The new case involves the same parties and the same claims already settled and closed with prejudice, so it is barred. Reviving those claims would also breach the parties' undertaking to comply with the agreement in utmost good faith.
alac.conclusion: The new case should be dismissed on the ground of res judicata.

notes: Decision based on a compromise agreement. It lays down no new doctrine and does not review the merits of the CA's Amended Decision (March 14, 2016) directing the NCIP to issue a Certification Precondition. The Civil Code articles (1306, 2028, 2037) and IPRA Section 59 cited in the doctrine's second paragraph and the suggested answers are basic law supplied for bar purposes; the decision itself does not cite them. The agreement's reference to "Administrative Order No. 03 series of 20212" is reproduced in the source as written (an evident typographical error). The compromise was signed by Macroasia Mining Corporation as assignee and authorized representative of respondent Macroasia Corporation.
